title: Abu Talib's house
hook: his uncle, poor and with many children, raises him as his own

segments.voice: Yesterday, the grandfather's rug in the Ka'ba's shade. Your line was: a place beside the elder.

One more grave. The old man who spread his rug by the Ka'ba dies too, the sirah says, while the boy is still young. Before he goes, Abd al-Muttalib asks one of his sons to take the orphan in. He chooses Abu Talib, the full brother of the boy's father, Abdullah, born of the same mother. And Abu Talib's house is already crowded, and his purse is thin. Today: Abu Talib.
screen: `THE GRANDFATHER DIES.` → `HE ENTRUSTS THE BOY.` → `A CROWDED HOUSE, A THIN PURSE.`

segments.voice: The sirah describes Abu Talib as a man of little money and a full house. Taking the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in means one more mouth at a table that's already stretched. He takes him anyway, and the sirah remembers his love for the boy. Ibn Ishaq says Abu Talib kept the boy close, and would take him along where he went. Notice the shape of this. The boy has lost a father he never saw, a mother on the road, and now a grandfather. Each time, someone stands in the gap. Halimah, who took the baby nobody wanted. Umm Ayman, who carried him home from Abwa. Abd al-Muttalib, on the rug. Now an uncle who can't really afford it. The Qur'an later speaks to the Prophet about exactly this. In surah ninety-three it reminds him that he was an orphan who was sheltered, and then it draws the line from his past to his duty. Pickthall translates: "Therefore the orphan oppress not." What was done for him, he is to do for others. And the story comes full circle in his own life. Years later, Ibn Ishaq says, when hard times fell on Quraysh and Abu Talib's family was struggling, Muhammad went to his uncle al-Abbas and proposed that each of them take one of Abu Talib's sons to ease the load. Muhammad took Ali, and raised him in his own home. The boy who was given room became the man who made room.
screen: `LITTLE MONEY, A FULL HOUSE.` · `ABU TALIB KEPT HIM CLOSE.` · `"THE ORPHAN OPPRESS NOT."` · `LATER, HE TAKES IN ALI.` · then, large: `THERE WAS ROOM.`

segments.voice: Who made room for you when it cost them something: a relative who took you in, a teacher who stayed late, a friend who shared a small apartment? Let one person come clearly to mind, the table or the couch or the car, and say thank you to them in your heart, plainly, as if they were sitting across from you. If you pray, you can ask Allah to reward them; if not, just let the thanks be full.
Abu Talib. The Prophet's uncle, a man of little money and a full house, who took the orphan in after his grandfather died, and kept him close. Today's word.
Your line: there was room. Tomorrow, the shepherd in the hills. See you then.

howItsDone: Muslims remember Abu Talib as the uncle who raised and protected the Prophet ﷺ, and care for orphans is taught from surah 93 and from the Prophet's own childhood.

chat.says: Who raised the Prophet after his grandfather died?
options: His uncle Abu Talib, a man of little money and a full house, who kept him close.
Halimah took him back to the desert and raised him with her own son.
His uncle al-Abbas, the one who later took in Ali to ease the load.
chat.meaning: The sirah says Abd al-Muttalib entrusted him to Abu Talib, who took him in despite little money, and kept him close.

sources.ref: Qur'an 93:6 (found thee an orphan and protected)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (Abd al-Muttalib's death; Abu Talib's guardianship; Muhammad takes in Ali in a time of hardship)

notes: The index hook says 'many children'; the script says 'a full house' without a count. Confirm.
Abu Talib as full brother of Abdullah (same mother, Fatimah bint 'Amr) per Ibn Ishaq; confirm.
The grandfather's age at death and the boy's age (sirah: eight) are left out under the claims rule.
The al-Abbas / Ali episode is from Ibn Ishaq; confirm it is placed in a time of hardship for Quraysh and that al-Abbas took Ja'far.
Pickthall 93:9 ('Therefore the orphan oppress not,') quoted from memory; confirm.
Abu Talib's faith is a matter on which Sunni and Shi'a scholars differ; the script stays with his care for the Prophet and makes no claim either way.
